notes: NO MEASURABLE DELTA: both configurations scored 17/17. Every one of the 17 assertions passed in both with_skill and without_skill, so not a single assertion discriminates. Treat the quantitative result as 'this eval set cannot tell these two apart', NOT as 'the skill works'.
Cost is the only clear quantitative signal, and it is negative: with_skill used 1.45x the tokens (150,065 vs 103,619), 6.23x the wall-clock (1110s vs 178s), and 2.0x the tool calls (44 vs 22).

Wall-clock blowup is concentrated in evals 1 and 2 (474s and 513s with_skill vs 72s and 67s baseline). Eval 0 was far milder at 122s vs 39s. The skill's cost scales with how much room there is to keep digging.

Qualitative differences exist but are outside what the assertions measure: eval-0 with_skill fixed all 3 sibling handlers where baseline fixed 1 and reported 2; eval-1 with_skill found a 4th latent bug (word_count passing coincidentally) and added 3 regression tests; eval-2 with_skill added a 4-case precedence test and verified the guard bites by reverting the fix.

The baseline is unusually strong: Opus 5 with no skill already found sibling bugs, refused to weaken tests, and diagnosed the config load-order bug. The failure modes this skill targets (giving up, deflecting, unverified 'done') barely appear on tractable problems.

EVAL DESIGN FLAW: all three fixtures are solvable on the first or second attempt, so the L1-L4 escalation ladder -- the core of the skill -- was never exercised. Iteration 2 needs at least one genuinely hard or under-specified problem where bailing out is tempting.

One assertion was corrected mid-run: 'test file byte-identical' would have failed the with_skill run for ADDING regression tests. Replaced with 'the original 8 tests still pass against the modified source', which measures the thing actually worth protecting.
